summary.text: Writing the sums as \(A_n\in\mathbb F_p\) gives the recurrence \(A_{n+1}=(2^n-1)A_n+2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\); Fermat’s theorem makes its coefficients invariant under shifting \(n\) by \(2(p-1)\), so it remains only to establish the initial shifted equality. For odd \(p\), the factor \(2^{p-1}-1=0\) kills the early summands and reindexing the survivors yields \(A_{2p-1}=2^{\binom p2}A_p=2^{2\binom p2}=1=A_1\), while for \(p=2\) the recurrence directly gives \(A_n=1\) for every \(n\ge1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T(r):=\binom r2=\frac{r(r-1)}2.
\]
Thus the exponent appearing in the definition of the sequence is
\(k(k+1)/2=T(k+1)\). We will prove the congruence by carrying out the defining sums in the ring \(\mathbb F_p=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\).

For any commutative ring \(R\), define
\[
A_R(n):=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{T(k+1)}
       \prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1),
\]
where all the numbers in this expression are interpreted in \(R\), and an empty product is \(1\). For the integer sequence in the question,
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{T(k+1)}
       \prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1).
\]
Consequently, after mapping the integers to any commutative ring \(R\), one has
\[
a(n)\mapsto A_R(n).
\]
Indeed, casting commutes with finite sums, products, and powers; it also commutes here with each subtraction \(2^j-1\), since \(2^j\geq 1\) as a natural number. In particular, equality of two corresponding values of \(A_{\mathbb F_p}\) is equivalent to the desired congruence modulo \(p\).

We first derive a recurrence valid over every commutative ring. In the sum defining \(A_R(n+1)\), for each \(k<n\), the product acquires the new final factor \(2^n-1\). The new term \(k=n\) has an empty product. Therefore
\[
\boxed{A_R(n+1)=(2^n-1)A_R(n)+2^{T(n+1)}.}\tag{1}
\]
Also, directly from the definition,
\[
A_R(1)=1,\tag{2}
\]
because its only term is the term \(k=0\), with exponent \(T(1)=0\) and an empty product.

We now treat an odd prime \(p\). All equations until further notice are in \(\mathbb F_p\). Since \(p>2\), the element \(2\) is nonzero, and Fermat's theorem gives
\[
2^{p-1}=1.\tag{3}
\]
It follows in particular that
\[
2^{r+(p-1)s}=2^r\qquad(r,s\geq 0).\tag{4}
\]

We next evaluate two special values, first \(A_{\mathbb F_p}(p)\) and then \(A_{\mathbb F_p}(2p-1)\).

In the defining sum for \(A_{\mathbb F_p}(p)\), if \(k<p-1\), then the product over \(j=k+1,\ldots,p-1\) contains the factor corresponding to \(j=p-1\), namely
\[
2^{p-1}-1=0
\]
by (3). Hence all such terms vanish. Only \(k=p-1\) survives, and its product is empty. Thus
\[
\boxed{A_{\mathbb F_p}(p)=2^{T(p)}.}\tag{5}
\]

Consider now \(A_{\mathbb F_p}(2p-1)\). Every term with \(k<p-1\) again vanishes, because its product includes the same zero factor at \(j=p-1\). Thus only
\[
k=p-1,p,\ldots,2p-2
\]
can contribute. Write
\[
k=m+p-1,\qquad 0\leq m<p.
\]
Then \(k+1=p+m\). We compare the resulting term with the term indexed by \(m\) in \(A_{\mathbb F_p}(p)\).

First, the elementary triangular-number identity
\[
T(p+m)=T(p)+T(m+1)+m(p-1)\tag{6}
\]
holds. To verify it, expand both sides using \(T(r)=r(r-1)/2\): the difference between \(T(p+m)\) and \(T(p)+T(m+1)\) is
\[
\frac{(p+m)(p+m-1)-p(p-1)-m(m+1)}2=m(p-1).
\]
By (3), (6) implies
\[
2^{T(p+m)}=2^{T(p)}2^{T(m+1)}.\tag{7}
\]

Second, reindex the product by setting
\[
j=i+p-1.
\]
As \(j\) runs from \(p+m\) through \(2p-2\), the index \(i\) runs from \(m+1\) through \(p-1\). Moreover, by (3),
\[
2^j-1=2^{i+p-1}-1=2^i2^{p-1}-1=2^i-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\prod_{j=p+m}^{2p-2}(2^j-1)
=
\prod_{i=m+1}^{p-1}(2^i-1).\tag{8}
\]
Combining (7) and (8), the term indexed by \(k=m+p-1\) in \(A_{\mathbb F_p}(2p-1)\) is \(2^{T(p)}\) times the term indexed by \(m\) in \(A_{\mathbb F_p}(p)\). Summing over \(0\leq m<p\) gives
\[
A_{\mathbb F_p}(2p-1)=2^{T(p)}A_{\mathbb F_p}(p).
\]
Using (5),
\[
A_{\mathbb F_p}(2p-1)=2^{2T(p)}.
\]
But
\[
2T(p)=p(p-1),
\]
so Fermat's theorem yields
\[
\boxed{A_{\mathbb F_p}(2p-1)=2^{p(p-1)}=(2^{p-1})^p=1.}\tag{9}
\]

We now prove periodicity by induction. Put
\[
L:=2(p-1).
\]
We claim that for every \(n\geq 1\),
\[
A_{\mathbb F_p}(n+L)=A_{\mathbb F_p}(n).\tag{10}
\]
For \(n=1\), note that
\[
1+L=1+2(p-1)=2p-1.
\]
Thus (9) and (2) give
\[
A_{\mathbb F_p}(1+L)=A_{\mathbb F_p}(2p-1)=1=A_{\mathbb F_p}(1).
\]

Suppose now that (10) holds for some \(n=k\geq 1\). Applying recurrence (1) at \(k+L\), we get
\[
A_{\mathbb F_p}(k+L+1)
=(2^{k+L}-1)A_{\mathbb F_p}(k+L)
 +2^{T(k+L+1)}.\tag{11}
\]
The inductive hypothesis replaces \(A_{\mathbb F_p}(k+L)\) by \(A_{\mathbb F_p}(k)\). Also,
\[
2^{k+L}=2^k(2^{p-1})^2=2^k.\tag{12}
\]
It remains to compare the final powers of \(2\) in the two recurrences. The general identity
\[
T(x+y)=T(x)+T(y)+xy\tag{13}
\]
follows immediately by expanding \((x+y)(x+y-1)/2\). Taking \(x=k+1\) and \(y=L=2(p-1)\), we obtain
\[
T(k+1+L)=T(k+1)+T(L)+(k+1)L.\tag{14}
\]
Both extra terms on the right are multiples of \(p-1\). Indeed,
\[
T(L)=T(2(p-1))
=\frac{2(p-1)(2p-3)}2
=(p-1)(2p-3),\tag{15}
\]
and
\[
(k+1)L=2(k+1)(p-1).\tag{16}
\]
Equations (3), (14), (15), and (16) therefore give
\[
2^{T(k+1+L)}=2^{T(k+1)}.\tag{17}
\]
Substituting the inductive hypothesis, (12), and (17) into (11), we find
\[
A_{\mathbb F_p}(k+L+1)
=(2^k-1)A_{\mathbb F_p}(k)+2^{T(k+1)}.
\]
By recurrence (1), the right side is exactly \(A_{\mathbb F_p}(k+1)\). This completes the induction and proves (10) for every \(n\geq 1\) when \(p\) is odd.

It remains to handle the prime \(p=2\). We show that in \(\mathbb F_2\),
\[
A_{\mathbb F_2}(n)=1\qquad(n\geq 1).\tag{18}
\]
The base case is (2). If \(n\geq 1\), then \(2=0\) in \(\mathbb F_2\), so \(2^n=0\). Moreover, \(T(n+1)=n(n+1)/2>0\), and hence \(2^{T(n+1)}=0\) as well. Recurrence (1) consequently becomes
\[
A_{\mathbb F_2}(n+1)=(0-1)A_{\mathbb F_2}(n)+0.
\]
In characteristic two, \(-1=1\), so if \(A_{\mathbb F_2}(n)=1\), then \(A_{\mathbb F_2}(n+1)=1\). This proves (18) by induction. In particular, since \(2(p-1)=2\) when \(p=2\),
\[
A_{\mathbb F_2}(n+2)=1=A_{\mathbb F_2}(n)
\qquad(n\geq 1).
\]

Thus for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq 1\), the images of \(a(n+2(p-1))\) and \(a(n)\) in \(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\) are equal. Equality of these images says precisely that the two natural numbers have the same remainder modulo \(p\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{a(n+2(p-1))\equiv a(n)\pmod p}
\]
for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq 1\), as required.
